title: Social Security Number collection - authority, notice, and the test
source: AUTHORED for MycOS 2026-08-30. The Privacy Act text is held in this corpus at 5 U.S.C. 552a. Section 7 of Pub. L. 93-579 is uncodified and appears as a note; its content is summarised here from the public law. The DoDI 1000.30 entry rests on the principal's account and is marked unverified. Not authority - a test to run, with the sources named so each step can be checked.
authority_class_basis: authored 2026-08-30; statute summarised, agency instruction unverified

sections.text: SSN collection - the authority chain. Three layers, and they are commonly cited in the wrong order. (1) The PRIVACY ACT OF 1974 is the public law. (2) EXECUTIVE ORDER 9397 is why SSN use spread across government, and it has been amended to remove the direction. (3) An agency's own implementing instruction - for DoD, DoDI 1000.30 - is where the written justification requirement lives. An instruction is not the source of the obligation; it is how one agency discharges it.

Privacy Act section 7. THE SSN PROVISIONS ARE NOT IN 5 U.S.C. 552a. This is the technical point that defeats most people who go looking: section 7 of the Privacy Act of 1974, Pub. L. 93-579, 88 Stat. 1896, was NEVER CODIFIED. It appears as a statutory NOTE to 5 U.S.C. 552a. Searching the section text for 'social security' returns nothing, and the provision is nonetheless law. s 7(a)(1): unlawful for any FEDERAL, STATE OR LOCAL agency to deny an individual any right, benefit or privilege provided by law because of refusal to disclose an SSN. s 7(a)(2): does not apply where disclosure is required by federal statute, or to a system of records in existence and operating before 1 January 1975 under a statute or regulation adopted before that date to verify identity. s 7(b): an agency requesting an SSN MUST tell the individual (i) whether disclosure is MANDATORY OR VOLUNTARY, (ii) BY WHAT STATUTORY AUTHORITY it is solicited, and (iii) WHAT USES will be made of it. Note what s 7(b) does in practice: an agency with no statutory authority cannot give the required notice truthfully, so the notice obligation and the authority requirement collapse into one test.

Executive Order 9397. Issued 22 November 1943, directing federal agencies to use the SSN as the numerical identification system for individuals - the reason SSN use became universal across government. AMENDED BY EXECUTIVE ORDER 13478 (18 November 2008), which removed the direction to use it, leaving agencies permitted rather than required. This matters when an agency answers 'EO 9397' to the question of authority: since 2008 that order directs nothing, and an executive order is in any event not the 'statutory authority' s 7(b) asks for.

DoDI 1000.30. Reduction of Social Security Number (SSN) Use Within DoD. Issued 1 August 2012; INCORPORATING CHANGE 2, 30 NOVEMBER 2022. Office of primary responsibility is now ATSD(PCLT) - the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Privacy, Civil Liberties, and Transparency - not USD(P&R) as at issue. It incorporates and cancels DTM 07-015. READ IN FULL 2026-08-30 and held in this corpus; the wording below is verbatim. THE OPERATIVE CLAUSE, verified: 'If upon review, it is determined that no authority or legal requirement for the use of the SSN exists, its collection and use should cease until such authority can be obtained.' THREE MORE LINES THAT DO MORE WORK THAN THAT ONE: (1) 'Any uses of the SSN not provided for in this Instruction are considered to be unnecessary and SHALL BE ELIMINATED.' - mandatory, not precatory, and it reverses the burden: a use is unnecessary unless the instruction provides for it. (2) 'The requirement for the use of the SSN provided by Executive Order 9397 has been ELIMINATED.' - DoD says this itself, so an agency answering EO 9397 is citing an authority its own department has disclaimed. EO 9397 'may be used to justify the use of the SSN as an interim measure while its use is being eliminated, but MAY NOT BY ITSELF BE USED TO JUSTIFY CONTINUED USE.' (3) 'Ease of use or unwillingness to change are not acceptable justifications', and systems or forms claiming 'operational necessity' SHALL BE CLOSELY SCRUTINIZED. SCOPE, and it matters: this instruction binds DoD COMPONENTS. It confers no rights on the public and is not the source of the obligation - the Privacy Act is. Cite it to show a DoD component failed its own mandatory standard, not as a statute a private party can sue on.

sections.text: the SSN test. To test any SSN collection, in this order: (1) IS THERE A FEDERAL STATUTE requiring or authorising disclosure for this purpose - not an executive order, not an agency convenience, not long practice. (2) WAS THE s 7(b) NOTICE GIVEN, stating mandatory or voluntary, the authority, and the uses. (3) WAS A RIGHT, BENEFIT OR PRIVILEGE DENIED for refusing - that is the s 7(a)(1) prohibition and the sharpest of the three. (4) IF THE COLLECTOR IS NOT AN AGENCY - a landlord, an employer, a private company - s 7 does not reach them at all: it binds federal, state and local agencies. Aim the argument at the right party.

sections.citation: SSN - what the remedy actually is
sections.text: SSN - what the remedy actually is. A caution against overreach, because the strength of the underlying point invites it. The civil remedy in 5 U.S.C. 552a(g) attaches to specified failures by an AGENCY as to records in a system of records, with actual damages and a wilful-or-intentional standard for the statutory minimum. Section 7 creates duties without spelling out its own damages remedy, and courts have divided on what follows from a bare s 7(b) notice failure - some treat it as supporting relief, others find no private right of action for section 7 alone. So: a missing justification memo is a real, auditable compliance failure and good leverage in a complaint to the agency or an IG; it is not automatically a damages claim. State it as the compliance gap it is.
